title: The Phantom of the Opera
author: Gaston Leroux
summary: Na Ópera de Paris, bailarinas sussurram sobre um fantasma de casaca preta que vive nos porões, exige um camarote só para ele e ameaça os novos diretores. Ao mesmo tempo, a jovem cantora Christine Daaé conquista o público com uma voz que parece ter sido ensinada por um “Anjo da Música” invisível. O visconde Raoul de Chagny, amigo de infância de Christine, começa a investigar esse mistério e descobre que, por trás das cortinas douradas, há um mundo escuro de lagos subterrâneos, armadilhas e uma paixão perigosa.

chapters.title: The Ghost
paragraphs: On the evening when the two old managers of the Paris Opera were giving their farewell performance, the dressing room of the little dancer Sorelli was suddenly invaded by half a dozen frightened girls from the ballet. Some were laughing nervously, others were crying, and all of them were trembling.
“It's the ghost!” cried little Meg Giry, shutting the door and leaning against it. “We saw him, in the passage. He came out of the wall!”
Sorelli, the leading dancer, was a tall, beautiful girl who liked to look calm. “Nonsense,” she said. “Ghosts don't exist.”

“But everyone has seen him,” said another girl. “He wears evening dress, like a gentleman. And he has no nose, and his eyes are two black holes, like a skull. Joseph Buquet, the scene shifter, saw him close up. He says the ghost's skin is yellow and stretched over his bones like an old drum.”
“Joseph Buquet talks too much,” said Meg. “My mother says the ghost doesn't like people who talk too much.”
Meg's mother, Madame Giry, was the woman who looked after the private boxes on the first tier. She often spoke of the ghost with great respect, and she said that Box Five belonged to him.
At that moment there was a sound of running footsteps in the passage, and a voice cried, “Joseph Buquet is dead! They've found him in the third cellar, hanging between two pieces of scenery!”
The girls screamed. Then they ran out to see. It was true. The poor man had been found hanging by a rope, but when people went down again to look, the rope had disappeared.

That same evening, upstairs, the performance was a triumph. The great singer Carlotta was ill, and her part was sung by a young, unknown Swedish singer called Christine Daaé. Nobody had ever thought she had much talent. But that night she sang like an angel. Her voice was so pure, so strong and so full of feeling that the whole audience rose to its feet, and many people were crying. When it was over, Christine fainted in the arms of her friends.

In one of the boxes sat the Count Philippe de Chagny and his younger brother, the Viscount Raoul, a handsome young naval officer of twenty-one. Raoul was very pale. He had recognised Christine at once.
“It is she,” he said to his brother. “Little Christine. I knew her when we were children.”
“Then go and congratulate her,” said Philippe, smiling, “but don't fall in love with a singer. Our family would not approve.”

Raoul hurried backstage and found Christine's dressing room. The door was open, and a doctor was helping her to recover. When she opened her eyes and saw Raoul, she looked at him for a moment and smiled.
“Monsieur,” she said, “who are you?”
“Christine, I am the little boy who went into the sea to bring back your scarf.”
She laughed, but a little nervously. “I don't remember you,” she said. “Please, everybody, leave me now. I am very tired.”

Raoul went out, hurt and confused. But he did not go far. He waited in the dark passage, hoping to speak to her later. When the others had left, he came back towards her door, and he was about to knock when he heard a man's voice inside. It was a strange voice, deep and beautiful, and very commanding.
“Christine, you must love me!” said the voice.
And Christine answered, in a voice trembling with fear and love, “How can you say that? When I sing only for you! Tonight I gave you my soul, and I am dead.”

Raoul stepped back into the shadows. A few minutes later the door opened, and Christine came out alone, wrapped in her furs, and went away. Raoul rushed into the room, determined to find his rival. It was empty. He searched everywhere, behind the curtains, in the cupboard, and under the table. There was nobody. The room had only one door, and nobody had come out of it except Christine.

chapters.title: Box Five
paragraphs: The next day the two old managers handed over the Opera to the new managers, Monsieur Moncharmin and Monsieur Richard. At the end of the meeting, the old managers looked at each other, a little embarrassed.
“There is one more thing,” said one of them. “The ghost.”
Richard laughed. “The ghost? You are joking.”

“Not at all. The ghost has certain demands. They are written in the contract book of the Opera. Box Five on the first tier must always be kept for him, at every performance. And he must be paid twenty thousand francs a month.”
The new managers thought this was an excellent joke. They laughed and said goodbye. But the next morning they found a letter on their desk, written in red ink, in a strange, childish hand.

“Dear Managers,” it said, “I am glad to see that you have kept my box free, as usual. But I must remind you about my monthly salary. Please be good enough to pay it to Madame Giry. Also, I wish Christine Daaé to sing the part of Marguerite in Faust next week. If you do not do as I ask, you will have a performance with a curse on it. Your obedient servant, O. G., the Opera Ghost.”
“Someone is playing a joke on us,” said Moncharmin. “Probably the old managers. We shall sell Box Five tonight.”

They did. But during the performance, the people in Box Five heard a voice beside them, laughing and making rude remarks, and nobody could be seen. They ran out in terror and complained to the managers.
The managers called Madame Giry, the box keeper. She was an old woman in a shabby black dress, with a bonnet on her head.
“Tell us about this ghost,” said Richard. “Have you seen him?”

“Nobody sees him, sir,” said Madame Giry. “But I hear his voice. He is very polite. He always leaves me a little present, some sweets or a few francs. He likes his box. He sits there during the performance, and nobody must disturb him. He doesn't like to be disturbed.”
“And where does he keep his evening dress?” laughed Moncharmin.
Madame Giry looked offended. “You may laugh, gentlemen,” she said, “but the old managers didn't laugh. They paid. And they had no accidents.”

The managers dismissed her and decided to do the opposite of everything the ghost asked. They refused to pay him. They gave the part of Marguerite to Carlotta, not to Christine. And they decided to sit in Box Five themselves during the performance, to show that they were not afraid.

That night, before the curtain went up, Carlotta received a letter. “If you sing tonight,” it said, “a great misfortune will happen to you, a misfortune worse than death.” Carlotta laughed and tore it up. She was a proud Spanish woman with a powerful voice, and she was not afraid of anyone.

The theatre was full. In Box Five, the two managers sat in the front row, looking around them with a superior air. The first act went well. Then Carlotta began her great song in the third act. Suddenly, in the middle of a beautiful high note, a horrible sound came out of her mouth.
“Co-ack!”

It was the sound of a toad. The audience froze. Carlotta stopped, her face white with horror. She tried again, and again the toad croaked. The managers felt a cold breath on the back of their necks, and they heard a voice say, quite close to them:
“She is singing tonight to bring down the chandelier!”

They both looked up at the ceiling. The enormous chandelier, made of crystal and bronze, weighing thousands of kilos, was moving. It was slipping down towards the audience. There was a terrible scream from two thousand people. Then the chandelier crashed down into the seats below. Many people were hurt. One woman was killed. She was the new concierge of the Opera, who had come to watch her first performance.

chapters.title: The Angel of Music
paragraphs: After the disaster of the chandelier, Christine disappeared. She did not come to the Opera, and nobody knew where she was. Raoul was desperate. He went to her little apartment every day, but she was never there. Then, one morning, he received a letter.
“Monsieur,” she wrote, “I have not forgotten the little boy who went into the sea to get my scarf. Tomorrow I am going to Perros, to visit my father's grave. If you wish, you may come too.”

Perros-Guirec was a little village on the coast of Brittany, by the grey sea. Raoul took the train that same evening. As the train rushed through the night, he remembered everything about his childhood friend.

Christine's father had been a poor Swedish peasant who played the violin better than anyone in Sweden. When his wife died, he took his little daughter and travelled around the country fairs, playing music while she sang. A professor heard them, and he brought them both to France. Every summer they went to Brittany, and the father played his violin on the beach while Christine sang.

One windy day, Christine's scarf blew into the sea. A little boy in a sailor suit ran into the waves, fully dressed, and brought it back. That boy was Raoul. After that, the three of them spent many happy days together. In the evenings, old Daaé told them the old legends of the north. His favourite was the story of the Angel of Music.

“Every great musician,” he used to say, “is visited at least once in his life by the Angel of Music. Sometimes the Angel comes to a child. The child hears a voice that nobody else can hear, and that voice teaches him to sing. After that, he sings like nobody else in the world.”
“Papa, have you heard the Angel of Music?” Christine asked.
“No, my child,” said her father. “But you will hear him one day. When I am in heaven, I will send him to you.”

Some years later, old Daaé fell ill and died in Paris. Christine was heartbroken. She went on studying at the Conservatoire, but she sang without joy, without soul. Raoul went away to sea and did not see her again until that night at the Opera.

The next day, at the inn of Perros, Raoul found Christine waiting for him. She was dressed in black and looked pale and tired. They walked together along the beach, and at last she told him her secret.

“The Angel of Music has come to me, Raoul,” she said. “Three months ago, in my dressing room, I heard a voice. It was the most beautiful voice in the world. It said that it was the Angel my father had promised to send. Since then, the Angel has given me lessons every day. That is why I sang so well that night. It was his voice that you heard in my room.”
Raoul looked at her in astonishment. Then he felt angry and jealous. “Christine,” he said, “you are being deceived. That was not an angel. That was a man. Someone is playing a cruel trick on you.”
Christine became white with anger. “How can you say that?” she cried, and she ran back to the inn.

That night Raoul could not sleep. Christine had said that she would go to her father's grave at midnight, to pray. Raoul followed her secretly through the snow to the little churchyard. The church stood alone beside the sea, and the wall of the churchyard was decorated with hundreds of skulls and bones, arranged in strange patterns. Christine knelt by the grave and prayed.

As the clock struck midnight, music began to play. It was a violin, and the melody was the one her father loved most, The Resurrection of Lazarus. It came from nowhere, from the air itself. Christine stood up, her arms open, as if she were in a dream. Raoul did not move. He was hiding behind a stone, and he was terrified.

When the music stopped, Christine walked out of the churchyard like a sleepwalker. Raoul came out of his hiding place and looked around. Suddenly some skulls rolled down from the wall at his feet. He looked up and saw a dark shape moving among the bones. He ran forward and seized a cloak.
“Who are you?” he shouted. “Show me your face!”

The figure turned. Raoul saw a terrible head, a head of death, with burning eyes. Then he received a violent blow, and everything went black. In the morning he was found lying on the steps of the church, almost frozen.

chapters.title: The Masked Ball
paragraphs: Raoul returned to Paris with a fever, and for several days he stayed in bed. When he recovered, he went straight to the Opera. Christine had returned and was singing again, more beautifully than ever. But whenever Raoul tried to speak to her, she turned away. She looked frightened, and her eyes were full of sadness.

Then, one morning, he received another letter from her. “There is a masked ball at the Opera on Tuesday night,” she wrote. “At midnight, be in the little room behind the chimney of the great foyer. Wear a white domino and a mask. As you love me, do not let anyone recognise you.”

On the night of the ball, the Opera was full of noise and colour. Hundreds of people in masks and fancy costumes were dancing, drinking and laughing on the grand staircase and in the foyers. Raoul, in his white domino, waited near the chimney. At midnight a black domino touched his arm. It was Christine.
“Follow me,” she whispered. “Quickly.”

As they crossed the crowd, Raoul noticed a strange figure. It was a man dressed all in scarlet, with an enormous hat with feathers, and a long red velvet cloak. His mask was a perfect skull. On the back of his cloak, in gold letters, were the words: “Do not touch me! I am Red Death passing by!” The dancers moved away from him in silence. One young man tried to touch him, but a bony hand seized his wrist with such strength that he cried out in pain.
Christine saw the red figure too, and she trembled. She pulled Raoul up the stairs into a small private room and locked the door.
“Raoul,” she said, “I have asked you to come because I must say goodbye. You must forget me. You must never come to my dressing room again. If you love me, do as I ask.”
“Christine, who is this man who frightens you? Is it the voice? Is it the Angel?”
She did not answer. “Goodbye, Raoul,” she said, and she ran out of the room.

Raoul did not obey her. He was too jealous and too worried. He went down to her dressing room before she arrived and hid behind the curtain that covered her dresses. A few minutes later Christine came in. She took off her mask, sat down in front of the large mirror, and put her head in her hands.
“Poor Erik,” she murmured.

Raoul did not understand. Who was Erik? At that moment, the voice began to sing. It came from everywhere and nowhere, from the walls, from the air. It was the most beautiful voice Raoul had ever heard. It sang the wedding night song from Romeo and Juliet, and its sound filled him with strange emotions, joy and terror at the same time.
“I am here, Erik,” said Christine softly. “I am ready.”

She rose and walked towards the mirror, as if she were hypnotised. Raoul watched her, unable to move. She walked into the mirror, and her image seemed to meet her there. Then the two Christines touched, and suddenly she was gone.

Raoul leaped from his hiding place. He ran to the mirror and pressed his hands against the cold glass. He saw only his own white face. He knocked on the walls and searched every corner, but he found nothing. The voice had stopped, and the room was silent.

For days after that, Christine did not appear. Raoul spent his time walking around the Opera, looking at every face and listening at every door. At last, one evening, he found her again. She was sitting alone on the stage, and when she saw him, she smiled sadly.
“I cannot stay away from you,” she said. “Erik has let me go free for a few days. Come, we will talk. But not here. Here, the walls have ears.”

She led him up and up, through endless stairs and passages, until they came out onto the roof of the Opera. Paris lay below them, with its thousands of lights. Above them, against the night sky, stood a great bronze statue of Apollo with his lyre.
“Here,” said Christine, “we are safe. Now I can tell you everything.”

chapters.title: Beneath the Opera
paragraphs: “The first time I went through the mirror,” Christine began, “was the night of the chandelier. I was in my dressing room, and the voice told me to come. I walked towards the mirror, and it seemed to turn. Suddenly I was in a dark passage. A hand took mine, a cold, bony hand. In the darkness I saw a man in a black cloak and a mask.

“He took me down, down, down, through the cellars of the Opera. There were five cellars, one below another, and he knew them all. At the bottom there was a white horse waiting. It was one of the horses from the opera stables. He lifted me onto it, and we went down further, along a path by the water. I felt like a girl in a fairy tale. I was not afraid. I was fascinated.

“Then we came to a lake. You will not believe me, Raoul, but there is a lake under the Opera, a huge, black, silent lake. The masked man helped me into a little boat, and he rowed across the dark water. All the time he was singing softly. At last we arrived at a door in the stone. He opened it, and I found myself in a small, comfortable house, full of flowers, with soft lamps and fine furniture. It was a house under the earth.
“There he took off his black cloak, but not his mask. He knelt in front of me and said, ‘Christine, I am not an angel, or a genius, or a ghost. I am Erik.’ And he began to cry.

“I understood then that he was a man, the man who had taught me to sing. I was angry and ashamed, but I also felt pity for him. He told me that he loved me. He told me that if I stayed with him, he would make me the greatest singer in the world. Then he promised that he would never touch me, and that I could leave whenever I wished.

“He kept his word. He was always polite and respectful. He sang to me, and he played the organ, the most wonderful music I had ever heard. He told me that he was writing an opera, Don Juan Triumphant, the greatest work of his life. When he sang, I forgot everything. I was in heaven.

“But I had one terrible desire. I wanted to see his face. On the second day, while he was playing the organ, I crept up behind him. My heart was beating wildly. Suddenly I reached out and tore off his mask.”
Christine stopped and covered her face with her hands. Raoul took her hand gently.
“Go on,” he said.

“Oh, Raoul, it was horrible. His face was a face of death. It was a skull with yellow skin. He had no nose, only a black hole. His eyes were deep in their holes, and they burned like two fires. His mouth was a dead, twisted thing. I screamed and fell back.

“He turned on me in a terrible rage. He seized my hands and pulled them towards his face, and he made me touch it. ‘Look!’ he shouted. ‘Look at me! You wanted to see me! Now you know! Now you can never leave me. Now you will stay here forever, with this corpse who loves you!’

“Then, suddenly, his anger disappeared, and he fell on his knees, crying like a child. He begged me to forgive him. He said that his own mother had never kissed him, that she had given him a mask when he was a baby, so that she did not have to see him. All his life, people had run away from him. He had lived as a monster at fairs, as a magician, and as an architect for kings in distant countries. At last he had come to Paris, and he had built this house under the Opera, where nobody would ever see him.

“After two weeks, he let me go back to the world. But first he made me promise that I would come back to him. He gave me a gold ring. ‘While you wear this ring,’ he said, ‘you will be safe from all danger. But you must stay faithful to me. If you love another man, Erik will know it, and Erik will be terrible.’”

chapters.title: Apollo's Lyre
paragraphs: When Christine had finished her story, Raoul held her in his arms. She was shaking with cold and fear.
“You will not go back to him,” he said firmly. “I love you, Christine. I will take you away from here, far away, where he can never find you.”
“Do you really love me, Raoul? Even though I am only a poor singer?”
“I would love you if you were a beggar in the street. Let us be engaged, Christine, from this moment. Nobody needs to know yet. It will be our secret.”
For the first time in many weeks, Christine laughed. “Yes,” she said, “we shall be engaged. Secretly engaged, like children.”

But then her face became serious again. “Raoul, you don't know Erik. He is a genius, but he is also mad. He can do anything. He can make his voice come from any place in a room. He knows every secret passage in this building. He has built traps that can kill a man. If he finds out about us, he will kill you.”
“Then we must leave as soon as possible.”

“Tomorrow night,” said Christine. “I am singing in Faust tomorrow. It will be my last performance. I promised him I would sing it. After the performance, take me away. Have a carriage waiting. Even if I refuse, even if I am afraid, take me by force.”
“I promise,” said Raoul. “Tomorrow at midnight, we will be free.”
They kissed, there on the roof under the stars. Then, hand in hand, they went towards the stairs. Suddenly Christine stopped and looked at her hand. She went pale.
“My ring!” she cried. “Erik's ring! I have lost it!” They searched everywhere, but they could not find it. “It is a bad sign,” she whispered. “Something terrible will happen.”

They did not know that someone had been listening to every word. High above them, on the great bronze statue of Apollo, a dark figure had been crouching in the shadows. When they left, the figure stood up. He held a small gold ring in his hand. He looked down at the place where the lovers had kissed, and he began to cry.
“Christine!” he moaned. “Christine!”
And the wind carried his sad cry over the roofs of Paris.
The next morning Raoul's brother, Count Philippe, called him into his study. Philippe was an older man, cold and proud, who had been like a father to Raoul since their parents died.

“I hear that you are leaving with that singer,” he said angrily. “The whole of Paris is talking about it. You are a Chagny, Raoul. You cannot marry a girl from the theatre. It would be a disgrace to our name.”
“I love her,” said Raoul. “I am going to marry her, whatever you say.”
“Then you are a fool,” said Philippe, and he left the room.

That evening Raoul went to the Opera. On his way to Christine's dressing room, he met a strange man in the passage. He was tall and dark, with green eyes and a black astrakhan cap. Everyone at the Opera knew him as the Persian. He came to every performance, but nobody knew his name or his business.

“Monsieur de Chagny,” said the Persian quietly, “I must warn you. You are in great danger. Erik knows everything. Do not talk to Christine again about running away. And never speak about the Opera Ghost.”
“What do you know about Erik?” asked Raoul.

“More than anyone else in the world,” said the Persian. “If ever you go down into the cellars of the Opera, remember one thing. Keep your hand always raised in front of your face, at the level of your eyes, as if you were going to fire a pistol. It may save your life.”
Before Raoul could ask any more questions, the Persian had disappeared into the crowd.

chapters.title: The Last Performance
paragraphs: The theatre was full that night. Everyone had come to hear Christine Daaé, and everyone was talking about the young Viscount de Chagny and the strange things that had happened at the Opera. Raoul sat in his brother's box, with a carriage waiting outside the Opera. Philippe sat beside him, cold and silent.

Christine had never sung so beautifully. In the last act, Marguerite is in prison, and she sings to the angels to save her soul. Christine raised her arms, and her voice rose higher and higher, so pure and so strong that the audience held its breath.
At that moment, all the lights in the theatre went out.
There was a cry of surprise from the audience, then shouting and confusion. The darkness lasted only a few seconds. When the lights came on again, the stage was empty. Christine had disappeared.

People began to shout. The singers ran around the stage, the stagehands searched behind the scenery, and the managers rushed out of their office. The police arrived within minutes. But nobody could find her. She had vanished, in front of two thousand people, in the middle of a song.
Raoul ran onto the stage, almost mad with fear. “Christine!” he cried. “Christine!” But there was no answer.
“It's the ghost,” whispered a little dancer. “The ghost has taken her.”

Raoul ran to Christine's dressing room. It was empty. He pressed against the mirror and beat on the walls with his fists, shouting her name. He knew where she was. She was down there, under the Opera, in the house by the lake, and Erik would never let her go again.
The police inspector, Monsieur Mifroid, had a different idea. He had heard the rumours about Raoul and Christine.

“Is it not true, Monsieur le Vicomte,” he asked, “that you intended to run away with Mademoiselle Daaé tonight? Perhaps your brother did not approve. Perhaps the Count de Chagny has taken her away himself, to stop the marriage.”

At that moment someone reported that Count Philippe had left the Opera in a great hurry, and that a carriage had been seen driving fast towards Brussels. Raoul did not believe that his brother had done it, but he did not have time to argue. He left the inspector's office and walked back through the dark passages, not knowing where to go.
In a corner of the passage someone was waiting for him. It was the Persian.

“Monsieur,” he said quietly, “are you going to look for Christine in Brussels? You will not find her there. She is here, very near, under our feet. Erik has taken her. If you want to save her, follow me. But I warn you, you may never come back.”
“I will follow you anywhere,” said Raoul.
“Then we must hurry. Erik has a plan. He wants Christine to marry him. If she refuses, I believe he will kill her, and perhaps many other people too.”

The Persian gave Raoul a pistol. “Remember,” he said. “Keep your hand at the level of your eyes. Erik's favourite weapon is the Punjab lasso, a thin cord of catgut that he throws around a man's neck in the dark. It kills silently. If your hand is raised, the cord will catch your hand and not your neck. That is how Joseph Buquet died.”

They went to Christine's dressing room, and the Persian began to press on the edges of the great mirror. After a few minutes, there was a click. The mirror turned slowly on a hidden axis, and a dark passage appeared behind it.
“This way,” whispered the Persian. “And not a word.”

chapters.title: The Persian's Story
paragraphs: They went down a narrow stone staircase in total darkness. The Persian carried a small lantern, but he covered it most of the time, so that only a thin line of light fell on the steps. The air became colder and damper. Somewhere far away, water was dripping.
“Who are you?” whispered Raoul. “And how do you know Erik?”

“I was once a chief of police in Persia,” said the Persian. “People there called me the Daroga. Many years ago, I met Erik at a fair in Russia, where he was showing his tricks. He was the greatest magician I had ever seen. He could throw his voice anywhere, he could sing like an angel, and he could build machines that nobody else could understand. I brought him to Persia, to the court of the Shah.

“The Shah gave him a palace to build. Erik built it full of secret doors and passages, so that the Shah could hear everything that was said in every room, and appear and disappear like a ghost. But Erik also built a torture room for the Shah's mother, a terrible room of mirrors, where people died slowly in the heat. Erik did many cruel things there. He killed many people with his lasso, for the amusement of the court.

“When the palace was finished, the Shah decided that Erik must die, so that nobody else would ever know its secrets. I was ordered to kill him. But I could not do it. I helped him to escape. Because of that I lost my position and my fortune, and I came to live in Paris. When I heard stories about the Opera ghost, I knew at once that it was Erik. I came to watch him, to make sure that he did not kill again. He promised me that he would stay quietly in his house by the lake. But now, because of his love for Christine, he has gone mad. I fear the worst.”
They reached the third cellar. It was an enormous, gloomy place full of old scenery, broken ropes and machines. The Persian stopped and listened.
“Hand at the level of your eyes,” he whispered. Raoul raised his pistol.

Suddenly a strange light appeared in the darkness, moving towards them. It was a head without a body, a head of fire. It floated through the air, a few feet above the ground. Raoul's hair stood on end.
“Don't move,” whispered the Persian. “It is not Erik.”

The fiery head passed close to them and disappeared. Later they learned it was only a rat-catcher with a lantern on his head, who went around the cellars every night with his rats. But at that moment, it was the most frightening thing Raoul had ever seen.
They went on, down to the fourth cellar, and then to the fifth. At last they came to the edge of the lake. The water was black and absolutely still.

“We cannot cross the lake,” said the Persian. “Erik has a siren there. If anyone tries to cross, he sings to them. His voice is so beautiful that men lean over the boat to listen, and then he pulls them under the water. I once nearly died that way myself. No, we must go another way, through the walls of his house.”

He led Raoul along a narrow passage between two walls. Then he stopped and felt the stones with his fingers. At last he found what he was looking for: a stone that moved. He pressed it, and a part of the floor opened beneath their feet. They fell together into darkness and landed hard on a smooth floor.

When the Persian lit his lantern, Raoul looked around. They were in a small room with six sides. Every wall was a mirror, from the floor to the ceiling. In the mirrors they saw themselves repeated a thousand times, a thousand frightened men with a thousand lanterns. In one corner was an iron tree, with iron branches.
The Persian's face had turned grey. “I know this room,” he said. “I know it from Persia. This is the torture room.”

chapters.title: The Torture Room
paragraphs: Through the wall they heard voices. One was Christine's, weak and frightened. The other was Erik's.

“You must decide, Christine,” said Erik. “I have been patient. I have waited long enough. I have made myself a new mask, a mask that looks like a real face. I will be like other men. We will be married, and we will go out on Sundays like everybody else. Don't you want that?”
“No,” cried Christine. “Let me go. I beg you.”

“Then I shall give you until eleven o'clock tomorrow night,” said Erik. “If you do not accept me as your husband, everyone will be dead and buried. Do you understand? Everyone. I am tired of living alone like a monster in a hole. I want to live like everybody else, with a wife of my own.” Then his voice changed. It became soft and sad. “Christine, why do you not love me? I love you so much.”
Then they heard a bell ringing somewhere, and Erik went out angrily. “Someone is at the lake,” he said. “I must go and see.”
Raoul shouted, “Christine! Christine! We are here!”
There was a cry of joy on the other side of the wall. “Raoul! Is it really you? Oh, you must go away. He will kill you.”
“Where are you?”

“I am in the room next to yours. He has tied me to a chair. He is mad, Raoul. He says that he will blow up the whole Opera. And he says that the room where you are is a torture room. Get out, get out quickly!”

At that moment the light in the room changed. It became brighter and brighter. The lamp in the ceiling was shining directly on the mirrors, and the room began to grow hot. Suddenly the mirrors were no longer mirrors. Around them, everywhere, there was a forest, a great tropical forest, with trees and leaves and lianas stretching away forever. It was an illusion created by the mirrors and the iron tree, but it looked completely real.
“Do not believe your eyes,” said the Persian. “It is a trick. The walls are still there.”

The heat became worse and worse. It was like being in the middle of an African desert under the midday sun. Raoul's tongue was dry, and his head was spinning. He saw rivers and lakes of cool water in the mirrors, and he ran towards them, but he only struck his head against the hot glass. Then the light changed again, and they were in a desert, with sand all around and a burning sun overhead.
Hour after hour passed. The two men were dying of thirst. Raoul lay on the floor, almost unconscious. He took out his pistol and put it to his head, but the Persian took it from him.
“Not yet,” said the Persian. “While we live, there is hope.”

The Persian began to examine the walls, inch by inch, searching for a secret door. He remembered that in Persia Erik always built a way out of his rooms. At last, in a corner, he found a small nail, slightly different from the others. He pressed it. A trapdoor opened in the floor, and a cool breath of air came up from below.

They climbed down a short ladder into a dark cellar. It was cold and silent. Raoul fell on his knees and thanked God. The Persian lit his lantern and looked around. Then he stopped, and his face turned white.
The cellar was full of barrels. He opened one of them and put his hand inside. When he took it out, it was full of black grains.
“Gunpowder,” he said in a whisper. “Enough gunpowder to blow up the whole Opera and half of Paris.”

chapters.title: The Scorpion or the Grasshopper
paragraphs: Above them, in Erik's house, they heard footsteps. Then Erik's voice came through the ceiling, loud and cheerful, as if he were telling a joke.

“Christine, my dear, it is almost eleven o'clock. You have had a whole day to think. Now you must choose. On the table, in the little box made of ebony, there are two small bronze figures. One is a scorpion. The other is a grasshopper. They look like toys, but they are not toys. If you turn the scorpion, it means yes. It means that you will be my wife, and that we shall go up into the world together. If you turn the grasshopper, it means no. And then the grasshopper will hop, oh, how it will hop! It will hop very high, and it will take the whole Opera with it.”

He laughed horribly. Below, in the cellar, Raoul and the Persian looked at the barrels of gunpowder around them. They understood. The grasshopper was connected to the gunpowder. If Christine turned it, everything would explode: the cellar, the theatre, and all the people who were sitting upstairs at that moment, watching the evening performance.
“I will leave you alone for five minutes,” said Erik. “When I come back, you will tell me. Scorpion or grasshopper.”
They heard a door close. Then Christine's voice came, very close, through a hole in the ceiling.
“Raoul! Are you there? Can you hear me?”
“Yes, Christine, we are here, in the cellar, under your feet. We have found the gunpowder.”
“Oh, Raoul, what shall I do? If I say no, everyone will die. If I say yes, I must marry him.”
The Persian spoke quickly. “Mademoiselle, you must turn the scorpion. Do it to save all those people. Do it to save us. Erik will not hurt you if you agree to marry him.”
There was a long silence. Raoul could hear Christine crying softly. Then they heard Erik come back into the room.
“Well, Christine?” he said. “Have you decided?”
“Erik,” said Christine, in a small, trembling voice, “I have turned the scorpion.”

At that very instant, they heard a strange sound in the cellar. It was water. Water was pouring in from a pipe in the wall, flowing around the barrels of gunpowder. Raoul and the Persian watched in horror as it rose: first to their ankles, then to their knees, then to their waists. Erik had flooded the cellar to make the gunpowder useless, and he had forgotten that there were men inside.
“Erik!” shouted the Persian. “Erik! Stop the water! We are drowning! It is I, the Daroga! You saved my life once. Save it now!”

The water rose higher and higher. It reached their chests, then their shoulders. They climbed onto the barrels, but the water continued to rise. Soon there was only a small space of air left under the ceiling. The two men pressed their faces against the stones, gasping for breath.
“Christine!” cried Raoul. “Christine!”
Then the Persian lost consciousness. The last thing he remembered was the black water closing over his head, and a strange, distant voice singing.

chapters.title: Erik's Story
paragraphs: When the Persian opened his eyes, he was lying on a soft bed in a small, elegant room. A lamp was burning, and the walls were covered with fine red curtains. Christine was standing beside him, silent and pale. And on a chair near the fire sat Erik, in his black evening clothes and his mask.

“Don't move, Daroga,” said Erik gently. “You are safe now. The young man is in the next room. He is alive too. When Christine turned the scorpion, I remembered you, and I opened the trapdoor. You were both almost dead.”
The Persian looked at Christine, but she said nothing. She looked like a woman in a dream. Then Erik gave him something to drink, and he fell asleep again.

When he woke up, he was in his own apartment in Paris. He did not know how he had got there. For several days he was ill with a fever, and his servant took care of him. He did not know what had happened to Raoul or to Christine.

Then, one evening, there was a knock at the door. His servant opened it, and a tall figure in a black cloak came in. It was Erik. He was thinner than ever, and he could hardly walk. He sat down heavily.
“Daroga,” he said, “I have come to tell you something. I am going to die soon. I am dying of love.”
The Persian looked at him in silence.

“Listen,” said Erik. “After I saved you, I sent you home. And I left the young man in a cellar, tied up, so that he could not do anything foolish. Christine stayed with me. She promised that she would not run away. She was my living bride, Daroga, my real living bride. She did not run away.

“That evening, I went to her, and I lifted my mask a little, just from my mouth, and I kissed her on the forehead. And she did not move away. She did not die of fear. She stayed there, like a real living bride. And then, Daroga, she kissed me too! She kissed me on the forehead, on my horrible forehead. Do you understand what that means? My mother never kissed me. She ran away from me. Nobody ever kissed me in my whole life, and Christine did.”
Erik was crying now, crying like a child, and his tears ran down under his mask.

“I fell at her feet,” he went on, “and I cried. And she cried too. Our tears mixed together. She took my hand, and she said, ‘Poor, unhappy Erik.’ I was so happy, Daroga, so happy! I felt like a man for the first time in my life.

“And then I understood that I could not keep her. A man who has received such a kiss cannot keep a woman like a prisoner. I went down to the cellar and set the young man free. I told him to take Christine and go, to marry her and be happy. I gave her the gold ring. I said, ‘Keep this as my wedding present to you.’ And I made her promise one thing: that when I died, she would come back secretly and bury me, with the ring on my finger. I told her that I would send her a sign.”
He stood up slowly. “Now I have told you everything. When I am dead, I will send you a sign too. Please put a notice in the newspaper, so that she will know. Goodbye, Daroga.”
And he went out into the night.

chapters.title: The End of the Ghost
paragraphs: Three weeks later, a short notice appeared in a Paris newspaper. It contained only two words: “Erik is dead.”

Christine Daaé and the Viscount Raoul de Chagny had disappeared from Paris. Nobody knew where they had gone. Some people said that they had gone to the far north, to some quiet country by the cold sea, where nobody had ever heard of the Paris Opera. Others said that they had married secretly and were living under another name. Christine never sang again in public.

The story of that terrible night had a sad ending for one other person. Count Philippe de Chagny, Raoul's brother, had not gone to Brussels after all. Worried about his brother, he had followed Raoul down into the cellars of the Opera, looking for him. Days later, his body was found on the bank of the underground lake. Nobody ever knew exactly how he had died. Perhaps the siren had called him. Perhaps he had simply drowned in the dark.

After that, the managers of the Opera never saw the ghost again. Box Five was sold like any other box. No more letters arrived in red ink. Little Meg Giry and the other dancers still told stories about the man in evening dress with the face of death, but they were only stories now. Madame Giry, the box keeper, always said that she missed him.
“He was a gentleman,” she said. “He never forgot my little presents.”

Many years later, the Opera was being repaired. Workmen were digging in the deepest cellars, near the place where the underground lake had been, to make a place to store the voices of great singers on gramophone records for future generations. In a hidden room, they found a skeleton. It was lying beside a little well. On one of its fingers there was a simple gold ring.

The newspapers said that it was one of the many victims of the Paris Commune, who had been killed in the cellars of the Opera in 1871. But the person who has written this story knows the truth. It is the skeleton of Erik, the Opera ghost. Christine kept her promise. She came back, secretly, and she put the gold ring on his finger before she left him forever in the house by the lake.

Who was Erik? He was a genius and a monster, a great musician, a great architect, a magician and a murderer. He had a heart large enough to hold the whole world, but he had to hide it behind a mask, because his face frightened everybody who saw it. All his life he wanted only one thing: to be loved like other men. In the end, he received a single kiss, and that kiss made him good.
So, if you visit the Paris Opera, and you hear a beautiful voice singing in an empty passage, do not be afraid. It is only the wind, perhaps. Or perhaps it is the ghost, still singing for Christine.
